LESSON 30 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

Digital Signatures, Certificates and PKI

How a signature proves origin and integrity, how a certificate binds a name to a public key, and how a chain back to a trusted root decides what a browser accepts.

Foundation15 min
Why this matters

A digital signature proves a key holder authorised a specific piece of data. A certificate binds an identity to a public key, and the public key infrastructure is the chain of trust that says who is allowed to issue those certificates.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Signing hashes the data and encrypts the hash with a private key, so the signature is bound to that exact content.
  • Verification uses the public key to recover the signed hash and compares it with a fresh hash of the received data.
  • A certificate contains a public key, an identity, and a signature from an issuer, so a relying party can check who vouched for the key.
  • A trust store holds the roots the client is willing to accept, and the chain from leaf to root is what makes an untrusted certificate acceptable.
  • Validation checks chain, dates, permitted uses and revocation, and a client that skips a step gains nothing from the scheme.

The background

  • Certificates were introduced with the public web because there was no way to know whom a public key belonged to.
  • Root certificates distributed with operating systems and browsers became the anchor of trust, and their compromise has repeatedly broken trust worldwide.
  • Certificate revocation has always been awkward, because a revoked certificate is a small amount of signed data that must be distributed reliably.
  • Certificate transparency was introduced to make issuance publicly auditable, so a mis-issued certificate can be spotted even before it is used.

Real-world examples

  • A certificate issued to the wrong name can let an impersonating server pass validation, which is why name checking is essential.
  • A device clock that is far out of step makes perfectly valid certificates look expired, so time accuracy is a security control.
  • Ignoring a certificate warning trains users to accept interception, which is how warnings get defeated in practice.

What to look for

  • Confirm the expected name is checked against the certificate, not just that a chain validates.
  • Check clock accuracy, since validation depends on it.
  • Check that warnings are treated as fatal rather than dismissible.
  • Look for internal certificates issued by a private authority, and confirm that authority is one you actually intend to trust.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use certificates from a reputable authority and automate renewal, so expiry is never a manual step.
  • Validate the full chain, the name, the dates and the permitted uses, and fail closed on any problem.
  • Keep the trust store small and current, since every root in it can issue for every name you visit.
  • Use certificate transparency monitoring for your own domains to catch a mis-issuance quickly.
  • Treat a bypassed certificate warning as an incident, not as a user inconvenience.
